source_text:
πολλάκις
γοῦν ἄριστα λόγον διεξεληλυθότος τινός, φαμὲν ὅτι οὗτος ἀληθῶς ἔμαθεν ἀφ' ὧν
εἴρηκεν λόγους, τοῦτ' ἔστι τῇ ἀγγελίᾳ καὶ τῇ φράσει βεβαίως ἔδειξε κατωρθωκέναι
τῶν λόγων τὴν μάθησιν.
{Hebr. 6,1} Μεθυπέρβατος ἡ ῥῆσίς ἐστιν· τὸ γὰρ διδαχῆς διὰ μέσου πρὸς ἅπαν
τὸ παρεγκείμενον ἀποδέδοται, καί ἐστιν ἡ κατὰ τὸν νοῦν αὐτῆς αὕτη συνθήκη· μὴ
πάλιν θεμέλιον καταβαλλόμενοι διδαχῆς, εἶθ' οὕτως τὰ καθ' ἐξῆς ἐν ἀπαριθμήσει
δηλούμενα περὶ ὧν τῆς διδαχῆς ὁ θεμέλιος.
orientation: The author is explaining the phrase 'he learned obedience through what he suffered' by comparing it to ordinary speech about someone who has mastered a discourse.
pass_a_gloss: For often, when someone has gone through a discourse excellently, we say that this man truly learned from the words he has spoken, that is, by the report and the phrasing he showed firmly that he had mastered the learning of the words. The saying is transposed; for the word 'of teaching' has been assigned through the middle to everything that lies alongside, and the arrangement according to its sense is this: not again laying down a foundation of teaching, then in this way the things in order being made clear in enumeration, about which things is the foundation of the teaching.

choices.why: The noun means announcement or message; 'report' fits the context of what someone has delivered in speech.
Phrasing captures the manner of expression, distinct from the content of the report.
The perfect infinitive of κατορθόω means to have brought something to a successful end; 'mastered' fits the context of learning.
The rare adjective describes a word order that has been moved around; 'transposed' is the literal sense.
The participle of παράκειμαι means what is placed beside; 'lying alongside' keeps the spatial metaphor of the grammatical explanation.
Here συνθήκη means the composition or ordering of words, not a covenant; 'arrangement' fits the grammatical context.

pass_b_english: At any rate, when someone has delivered a speech extremely well, we often say, “This man truly learned from the words he spoke”—that is, by his message and his phrasing he showed with certainty that he had mastered the learning of those words.

The saying in Hebrews 6:1 is transposed. The phrase “of teaching” has been placed in the middle and assigned to everything lying alongside it, and the arrangement according to its meaning is this: not laying down again a foundation of teaching—and then, in sequence, the items set out in the enumeration concerning which the foundation of the teaching exists.

problems.quote: by his report and his phrasing
problems.why: ἀγγελίᾳ here means 'message' or 'announcement', not 'report' in the sense of journalistic reporting; it refers to the content conveyed, not a secondary account.
problems.fix: by his message and his phrasing

edits.old: by his report and his phrasing
edits.new: by his message and his phrasing

problems.quote: the phrase "of teaching" has been placed in the middle and assigned to everything lying alongside it
problems.why: Technical discussion of Greek word order is opaque without original text; 'lying alongside it' meaningless.
problems.fix: Explain Greek hyperbaton or give literal then smooth translation.

problems.quote: the arrangement according to its meaning is this: not laying down again a foundation of teaching—and then, in sequence, the items set out in the enumeration concerning which the foundation of the teaching exists
problems.why: The 'arrangement' is supposed to clarify but is itself a convoluted fragment with dangling modifier.
problems.fix: Reconstruct the intended word order and give it first.

problems.quote: This man truly learned from the words he spoke
problems.why: Illogical: one learns FROM speaking words? Should be 'by' or 'through' the words he spoke, or 'showed mastery in'.
problems.fix: Clarify whether 'learned from' means 'was taught by' or 'demonstrated learning through'.

problems.quote: The saying in Hebrews 6:1 is transposed.
problems.why: Reader cannot tell who identifies this transposition—Gennadius or a source.
problems.fix: Frame as Gennadius's own observation about the Greek word order.

problems.quote: the items set out in the enumeration concerning which the foundation of the teaching exists.
problems.why: Compressed syntax obscures meaning: the foundation concerns the listed items.
problems.fix: Reword: 'the listed items on which the teaching's foundation rests.'

edits.old: This man truly learned from the words he spoke
edits.new: This man truly learned through the words he spoke

edits.old: The saying in Hebrews 6:1 is transposed. The phrase “of teaching” has been placed in the middle and assigned to everything lying alongside it, and the arrangement according to its meaning is this: not laying down again a foundation of teaching—and then, in sequence, the items set out in the enumeration concerning which the foundation of the teaching exists.
edits.new: Gennadius observes that the saying in Hebrews 6:1 is transposed: the phrase “of teaching” has been placed in the middle and assigned to everything lying alongside it. The arrangement according to its meaning is this: not laying down again a foundation of teaching—and then, in sequence, the items set out in the enumeration, which are the things on which the foundation of the teaching rests.

fixed: The mistranslation of 'learned from' is fixed to 'learned through'.
The speaker issue is fixed by attributing the observation to Gennadius.
The unreadable arrangement and enumeration are clarified by reworking the final clause.

problems.why: Third person suddenly; is this Gennadius or excerptor speaking?
problems.fix: Clarify attribution in source (self-reference or editorial?)

problems.quote: the phrase "of teaching" has been placed in the middle and assigned to everything lying alongside it
problems.why: Technical claim without visible text; 'lying alongside' obscure
problems.fix: Show Greek syntax or diagram the transposition

edits.old: Gennadius observes that the saying in Hebrews 6:1 is transposed: the phrase “of teaching” has been placed in the middle and assigned to everything lying alongside it.
edits.new: The saying in Hebrews 6:1 is transposed: the phrase “of teaching” has been placed in the middle and assigned to everything lying alongside it.

fixed: The speaker problem is real: the source has no explicit attribution to Gennadius, so the third-person attribution has been removed.
The unreadable problem is not a translation error: the English accurately renders the source's technical description of the transposition. No change made.

last_rejected.quote: The saying in Hebrews 6:1 is transposed
last_rejected.why: Brief requires 'Hebrews' not 'Hebr.' and same chapter/verse numbers; source has Hebr. 6,1, English has 6:1 with colon.
last_rejected.fix: The saying in Hebrews 6,1 is transposed
last_rejected.ruling: Hebr. 6,1 and 6:1 are equivalent reference formats; no meaning change or broken glossary.

last_rejected.quote: he showed with certainty that he had mastered the learning of those words
last_rejected.source_quote: τῇ ἀγγελίᾳ καὶ τῇ φράσει βεβαίως ἔδειξε κατωρθωκέναι τῶν λόγων τὴν μάθησιν
last_rejected.why: Greek says he showed he had successfully accomplished/mastered the learning; 'mastered the learning of those words' is awkward and slightly off—he demonstrated mastery through message and phrasing.
last_rejected.fix: by his message and his phrasing he firmly showed he had mastered the lesson of those words
last_rejected.ruling: κατωρθωκέναι means 'successfully accomplish/master'; 'mastered the learning' is within normal range.

last_rejected.quote: concerning which the foundation of the teaching exists
last_rejected.source_quote: περὶ ὧν τῆς διδαχῆς ὁ θεμέλιος
last_rejected.why: Greek says 'the foundation of the teaching' is concerning these things, not that it 'exists' concerning them; 'exists' adds an ontological claim absent in source.
last_rejected.fix: concerning which is the foundation of the teaching
last_rejected.ruling: Greek is elliptical; 'exists' supplies an English copula, not an ontological claim; meaning unchanged.
